This is a guideline for discussion, not an alpha-controlled test, and its false-alarm rate needs the same simulation report as any Bayesian rule. With a flat prior on the log hazard ratio the posterior is centered at the observed log hazard ratio, so the probability exceeds one half exactly when the observed hazard ratio exceeds 1.2, whatever the number of events: `r round(monitor_harm_rule(60, 1.2, Dmax = 60)$p_harm, 2)` at an observed 1.2 and `r round(monitor_harm_rule(60, 1.3, Dmax = 60)$p_harm, 2)` at 1.3 with 60 events. What the number of events changes is how quickly the probability moves away from one half. For futility the relevant quantity is the predictive probability of final success: at the second look the flat-prior predictive probability of crossing the final boundary of 2.02 is `r round(monitor_harm_rule(600, 0.83, Dmax = 1200, z_crit = 2.02)$pp_success, 2)`, so there is no case for futility. A real example of a monitored stop for harm after an excess of deaths is torcetrapib: Pfizer stopped the ILLUMINATE outcomes trial in December 2006 on the DMC's recommendation, and the signal (a rise in blood pressure) had been visible in earlier phases (see @sec-lifecycle).

### A reporting template for the DMC {.unnumbered}

The comparison suggests a short monitoring section that a sponsor can write and a regulator can accept.

1. State a group sequential efficacy boundary (or a calibrated Bayesian rule with its simulated or exact null error) that controls the type I error for regulatory purposes.
2. Report to the committee at each look the posterior probabilities of benefit and of clinically meaningful benefit under a flat and a skeptical prior, the posterior probability of harm, and the predictive probability of final success, each next to the boundary it is read against.
3. Report the anytime-valid Bayes factor with its direction condition ($Z > 0$) so that unscheduled looks prompted by safety concerns do not compromise the error guarantee.
4. State that the committee may decline to stop at a crossed boundary, and that it will explain its reasoning in the final report.

None of this requires a change in regulation. It requires that the committee be shown the quantities it uses to reason, instead of reconstructing them informally from a $z$ statistic.

## In practice {#sec-ch10-practice}

Four real trials show the chapter's ideas at work: what stopping early does to the estimate, a posterior probability used as a stopping rule, a futility stop under a group sequential design, and a stop for harm decided by a DMC.

### Truncated trials overestimate: Bassler and colleagues (2010)

Bassler and colleagues [@bassler2010truncated] matched 91 randomized trials that had been stopped early for benefit (asking 63 distinct questions) to 424 nontruncated trials from systematic reviews of the same questions. The pooled ratio of relative risks, truncated over nontruncated, was $0.71$ (95% confidence interval $0.65$ to $0.77$): the pooled relative-risk estimate in the truncated trials was on average 29 percent lower than in the matched nontruncated trials. The difference was independent of whether a statistical stopping rule was present and of methodological quality (allocation concealment, blinding), and it was greatest in smaller studies.

The size of the problem is debated. Montori and colleagues [@montori2005randomized] documented the pattern in a systematic review of trials stopped early for benefit, and Freidlin and Korn [@freidlin2009stopping] argue that the bias is smaller than such reviews suggest when the boundaries are conservative.

The lesson is the one in the DMC section. A boundary controls the type I error, but it does nothing for the point estimate at the moment of stopping, and a design with an O'Brien-Fleming boundary is not immune. The regulatory consequence is practical: a trial stopped early should report its estimate with the information fraction and the interval in view, and the protocol should say how the estimate will be read. A shrinkage prior is the Bayesian answer, and it is the subject of @sec-priors.

The frequentist answer is a bias-adjusted estimator. The maximum likelihood estimate after a sequential test is biased, which Whitehead [@whitehead1986bias] studied, and adjusted or median-unbiased estimators and intervals that respect the stopping rule are the standard remedy in group sequential software. The size of the effect is easy to see in a two-look design (@tbl-ch10-bias).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ch10-bias
#| tbl-cap: "A two-look O'Brien-Fleming design (one-sided 0.025, looks at half and full information, bounds 2.797 and 1.977) with true drift 2.5 on the Z scale. Estimates are on the drift scale, Z divided by the square root of the information fraction."
set.seed(7); m <- 2.5; B <- 2e5
z1 <- rnorm(B, m * sqrt(0.5), 1)
z2 <- (z1 + rnorm(B, m * sqrt(0.5), 1)) / sqrt(2); s1 <- z1 >= 2.797; s2 <- !s1 & z2 >= 1.977
est <- ifelse(s1, z1 / sqrt(0.5), z2)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Quantity = c("P(stop at the interim)", "Mean estimate, stopped at the interim", "Mean estimate, all trials that reject", "Mean estimate, all trials"),
  Value = c(mean(s1), mean(est[s1]), mean(est[s1 | s2]), mean(est))), digits = 2, align = "lr")
```

Trials that stop at the interim report an estimate far above the truth of 2.5, and the trials that reject at either look report one that is still too high, although the average over all trials, including those that never cross, is much closer to the truth (it is still a little high, because the interim stop freezes the estimate at its peak). The bias belongs to the selection that stopping implies, and Bayesian shrinkage can reduce upward selection bias, but its bias and interval coverage depend on the prior and should be evaluated under the stopping rule. Either way, the protocol should say which estimate will be reported at an early stop.

### A posterior probability as the stopping rule: therapeutic heparin in Covid-19 (2021)

The ATTACC, ACTIV-4a and REMAP-CAP trials ran as one multiplatform design, comparing therapeutic-dose heparin with usual-care thromboprophylaxis in two cohorts, with organ support-free days to day 21 (death scored $-1$) as the outcome. Randomization continued within each cohort until a posterior conclusion of superiority (more than 99 percent probability that the proportional odds ratio exceeded 1) or futility (more than 95 percent probability that it was below 1.2) was reached. The model was Bayesian cumulative logistic, with the two cohorts nested under a hierarchical prior with a neutral overall effect.

In critically ill patients enrollment stopped on 19 December 2020 at the futility criterion [@goligher2021anticoag]. Of 1207 randomized, primary outcome data were available for 1098. The adjusted odds ratio was $0.83$ (95% credible interval $0.67$ to $1.03$), with a posterior probability of futility of $99.9$ percent. Note what futility means here: the interval barely includes 1, and the criterion is defined against an odds ratio of 1.2, not against no effect. In non-critically ill patients the trial was stopped when its prespecified criteria for superiority were met [@lawler2021anticoag]. Of 2244 randomized, 2219 were analyzed, the probability that the therapeutic dose increased organ support-free days was $98.6$ percent, and the adjusted odds ratio was $1.27$ (95% credible interval $1.03$ to $1.58$).

The same rule gave opposite stops in two cohorts, and neither is a frequentist boundary. The comparison with this chapter is direct: the posterior is valid at any stopping time, but the operating characteristics of the rule (the chance of a false stop for benefit or futility) have to be shown by simulation, as in @sec-simulation. The group sequential alternative would have fixed the looks and the spending in advance.

### A futility stop and its reanalysis: EOLIA (2018)

EOLIA randomized 249 patients with very severe acute respiratory distress syndrome to early extracorporeal membrane oxygenation or conventional management [@combes2018]. Sixty-day mortality was 35 percent (44 of 124) against 46 percent (57 of 125), a relative risk of $0.76$ (95% confidence interval $0.55$ to $1.04$), $P = 0.09$. The trial was stopped for futility under a prespecified sequential design with a two-sided triangular test [@whitehead1983triangular], the design of @sec-ch10-families.

Goligher and colleagues [@goligher2018] reanalyzed the trial post hoc to show the effect of the prior. The posterior probability of any mortality benefit (relative risk below 1) was 96 percent under a minimally informative prior, 99 percent under a moderately enthusiastic prior, 88 percent under a strongly skeptical prior, and 99 percent under a prior built from published studies. But the probability of the 20-point absolute reduction the trial was powered for was only 2 percent under the minimally informative prior and 4 percent under the meta-analytic prior.

The lesson is that a frequentist futility stop and a Bayesian summary answer different questions. The first says the design target was unlikely to be reached. The second says benefit of some size is probable. Both can be true, and a decision maker needs both, which is the argument of @sec-evidence for reporting the posterior at several thresholds.

### A stop for harm: the Women's Health Initiative (2002)

The estrogen plus progestin trial of the Women's Health Initiative, in healthy postmenopausal women, was stopped early for harm, on the recommendation of its data monitoring committee, and the principal results were published in JAMA in July 2002 [@rossouw2002whi]. At the board's recommendation on 31 May 2002, after a mean of 5.2 years of follow-up, the test statistic for invasive breast cancer had exceeded the stopping boundary for that adverse effect and the global index statistic supported risks exceeding benefits. The estimated hazard ratios (nominal 95% confidence intervals) were $1.26$ ($1.00$ to $1.59$) for invasive breast cancer (290 cases), $1.29$ ($1.02$ to $1.63$) for coronary heart disease (286 cases), $1.41$ ($1.07$ to $1.85$) for stroke, and $1.15$ ($1.03$ to $1.28$) for the global index, while total mortality was not affected ($0.98$, $0.82$ to $1.18$). The nominal interval for breast cancer reaches $1.00$: the stop rested on the crossing of a sequential boundary, not on that interval.

Safety and harm monitoring in a trial of this kind is not a formal alpha-controlled test of a single endpoint. The committee weighs a pattern of outcomes, and a stop for harm is a decision under uncertainty made with discretion, which is what the DMC section of this chapter describes. The charter, the guidance on DMCs and the stopping guidelines exist so that such a decision can be made by people who see unblinded data and are independent of the sponsor.

## Key points {.unnumbered}

- Testing repeatedly at a fixed level is not a test: two equally spaced looks raise one-sided $2.5\%$ to about `r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * gs_power((1:2) / 2, rep(za, 2)))`$\%$, ten to about `r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * gs_power((1:10) / 10, rep(za, 10)))`$\%$, and, with monitoring continued indefinitely, the fixed cutoff is eventually crossed with probability one (finite-horizon crossing probabilities remain below one). The Armitage-McPherson-Rowe recursion computes the exact inflation and every boundary in the traditional toolbox.
- O'Brien-Fleming boundaries ($4.05, 2.86, 2.34, 2.02$ for four looks) cost about 2 percent in sample size and keep the final bar near $1.96$. Pocock boundaries (about $2.36$ throughout) stop earlier when the drug works and cost about 18 percent more patients if the trial runs to the end.
- Lan-DeMets spending fixes a function, not times: the boundaries follow the realized information fraction, provided the timing is not driven by the observed effect. Alpha is distributed, not consumed.
- Futility rules should be non-binding in confirmatory trials; power is computed as though they are obeyed. Binding rules buy back a little alpha at the price of validity if overridden.
- DMCs see unblinded data, recommend rather than decide, and treat boundaries as guidelines. Early-stopped estimates are biased upward.
- The posterior does not depend on the stopping rule, but the type I error does. A Bayesian monitoring rule can be perfectly calibrated under the prior and still reject a true null in about `r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * lk[4])`% of trials: its frequentist error is computed by simulation (@sec-simulation).
- The Bayes sequential problem is solved by backward induction on a sufficient statistic. Wald's SPRT is its two-point special case, with the large deviation ledger $n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \log(1/\alpha)$.
- The three tolls: $Z_n \ge z_\alpha$ (fixed level), $Z_n > 0$ and $Z_n^2 \ge (1+1/q)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log b\}$ (Bayes, approximately $\log n + C$ at large information) and the same with $b = 1/\alpha$ and $Z_n > 0$ (anytime valid for the normal mixture, approximately $\log n + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)$). The Bayes-factor bar is above the unadjusted bar once $I_n\tau^2 > 46$ ($n > 46$ for a unit-information prior), so the Bayesian saving is not against a single look. For the normal-mixture construction, against the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar, the approximate surcharge is $7.38/10.51 \approx 70\%$ of a conventional trial asymptotically (a comparison of boundary terms, not an exact sample-size identity); calibration narrows it (SELECT reconstruction, among trials that declare efficacy: a median of `r sr$median_events_success[3]` events for the calibrated Bayesian rule against `r sr$median_events_success[2]` for the e-value rule, with powers `r sprintf('%.2f', sr$power[3])` and `r sprintf('%.2f', sr$power[2])`).

::: {.callout-note title="Discussion questions"}
1. A sponsor proposes ten Bayesian looks, each stopping for efficacy if $\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid \text{data}) > 0.975$, and argues that the posterior "is not affected by looking". What would you ask for before accepting the design, and what do the numbers in @tbl-ch10-inflation and @tbl-ch10-likelihood suggest the answer will be?
2. A cardiovascular trial plans an O'Brien-Fleming-type design with looks at 50 and 75 percent of events, and the second look takes place at 68 percent because event accrual was slow. What does a Lan-DeMets design do, what would a fixed-boundary design have to do, and what would you check about why the look moved?
3. The DMC sees a crossing of the efficacy boundary at the first look, with a favorable trend on the primary endpoint and an unfavorable trend on all-cause mortality. Should the boundary be binding? How would the charter have to be written to give the committee the discretion it needs without compromising the type I error?
4. A futility rule is binding in the protocol and the DMC declines to follow it. What has happened to the type I error, and what can the sponsor say to the regulator?
5. The three tolls say the normal-mixture rule valid at every stopping time carries an approximate surcharge of seventy percent of a conventional trial against the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar, and `r round(100 * (sr$median_events_success[2] / sr$median_events_success[3] - 1))` percent more events at the median than a calibrated Bayesian rule in SELECT (among trials that declare efficacy). Under what circumstances is that worth paying, and under what circumstances is a four-look group sequential design the better purchase?
:::
